inline.s: [ To stop the infant's crying ] This is a metaphor for the expedient teaching (not the final teaching). When a child cries, an adult gives him a yellow poplar leaf, saying, ‘This is a gold piece; you may take it to buy sweets.’ The child holds it and stops crying. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
Volume Twenty,
says:

‘As when an infant cries, the parents give it a yellow poplar leaf and say: “Don't cry! Don't cry! I shall give you gold.” The infant, seeing it, thinks it is real gold and stops crying; yet this poplar leaf is not really gold.’
The Compendium of the Five Lamps further records:
The Chan master Zizai of Funiu Mountain at Yique, of the Li family of Wuxing, first followed the master Guoyi, and after receiving full ordination studied under Mazu and awakened to the mind-ground
(enlightenment)
. Mazu had him deliver a letter to the National Master Zhong
(National Master Huizhong)
. The National Master asked, ‘What Dharma does the great master Ma use to show his disciples?’ The master said, ‘
mind is Buddha
.’ The National Master said, ‘What kind of talk is that
(he greatly disapproved)
!’ After a long while
(a long time passed)
he asked again, ‘Besides this, is there any further teaching?’ The master said, ‘
not mind, not Buddha
. Or it is said:
neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing.
’ The National Master said, ‘That is a little closer
(that is about right)
In the kōan above three stages are set forth:
‘mind is Buddha’
‘not mind, not Buddha’
‘neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing’

. The ‘mind’ spoken of here refers to the self-nature. ‘Mind is Buddha’ means that the Buddha is nothing other than this: the self-nature that is fully awakened is the Buddha. ‘Not mind, not Buddha’ means that the self-nature and the Buddha are both illusions, doings within the dream of ignorance. ‘Neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing’ speaks of the one who dreams the dream of ignorance.
Q:
All sentient beings are originally Buddhas; since they are Buddhas, why do they give rise to ignorance and sink into being sentient beings?

Answer: All sentient beings originally possess the Tathāgata's wisdom and adorned nature, which is why they are said to be ‘originally Buddhas,’ yet there remains the fundamental ignorance in a latent state. Once it manifests (a single thought of non-awakening) and one enters the dream of ignorance, one sinks into being a sentient being. The process is: a single thought of non-awakening gives rise to the three subtle aspects, and the realm of objects serves as the condition for the growth of the six coarse aspects. (For details see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
Q: If ignorance is said to be originally present, then since ignorance exists, how can one be said to have attained Buddhahood?

Answer: Although the original Buddha has fundamental ignorance, that fundamental ignorance is in a latent state, and so he still possesses the Tathāgata's wisdom and adorned nature. Since he possesses the Tathāgata's wisdom and adorned nature, he is of course a Buddha.

Q: All sentient beings were originally already Buddhas, and later gave rise to ignorance, entered the dream of ignorance, and sank into being sentient beings. Now we are practicing — after we attain Buddhahood, at what time shall we again give rise to ignorance, enter the dream of ignorance, and sink into being sentient beings?

Answer: When we now practice to attain Buddhahood, the aim is to eradicate fundamental ignorance. So one who eradicates fundamental ignorance and attains Buddhahood will never again give rise to ignorance, enter the dream of ignorance, or sink into being a sentient being. This is like a man who, before he has had smallpox, is a healthy person; having had smallpox he falls into being a patient, and after he recovers he is again a healthy person and, indeed, with lifelong immunity, so he will never again contract smallpox. Concerning this, in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment the Buddha teaches:

‘Good man! As when ore is smelted with gold, the gold does not come into being because of the smelting; once it has become gold, it does not again turn to ore. … The Tathāgata's perfect enlightenment is likewise.’
(Translation: Good man! As when gold ore is smelted, the gold does not come into being because of the smelting; once it is smelted into pure gold, it will not again become ore.
The Tathāgata's perfect enlightenment is also thus (it does not reverse).)

[Fundamental ignorance] From the beginningless beginning a single thought of non-awakening causes one to enter the dream of ignorance, to be dazed through the long night, unable to understand the truth, and to give rise to all delusions and afflictions. This is fundamental ignorance, also called beginningless ignorance. The Mahāyāna Scripture of the Meaning of the Six Perfections says:

‘As the fierce flame of fire borne on the wind can be restrained, and the waves of the ocean can likewise be stilled, only the deluded mind is very hard to subdue. Why? Because from beginningless ignorance it is deluded about the nature of the mind.’
Q: ‘When the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease’ — what does this mean?
Answer:

‘When the mind arises, various dharmas arise’ means that the mind arises and one enters the dream of ignorance; ‘when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease’ means that the mind ceases and the dream of ignorance is awakened from. The Song of Realizing the Way says:
‘In the dream the six realms plainly show; once wakened, all the vast world is empty and hollow.’
The Mahāyāna Ghanavyūha Sutra says:
‘As the forms in a dream
(form-objects — the visible things)
are only deluded viewings of thought, on waking
(awakening from sleep)
they are without existence; [so too] while the dream of ignorance
and seeing the various forms of men and women and the like, upon perfect enlightenment there is nothing to be seen.’
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
‘This ignorance does not have a real substance, like a man in a dream — while dreaming it is not without, and upon waking nothing is obtained.’
The Sutra in Which the Buddha Speaks the Dharma of Kings to King Suvarṇaprabhāsa says:

‘All dharmas are empty in essence and nature, impermanent, decaying and destroyed. It is like a person who in a night dream sees fine gardens, mountains, rivers, crowds, dense forests, clear springs, halls, houses, towers, and pavilions, all delightful, and when he wakes
(awakening from sleep)
he sees nothing at all.’
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
Therefore the three realms are false and illusory, made by mind alone; apart from mind there are no six sense-object realms. What is the meaning of this? Because all dharmas arise from
mind giving rise to false thoughts

. All discrimination is the discrimination of one's own mind; mind does not see mind, and there is nothing to be apprehended. Know that all the realms of the world exist dependent upon the ignorant deluded mind of sentient beings. Therefore all dharmas, like images in a mirror, have no substance to be apprehended; they are only the mind's falseness,
because when the mind arises various dharmas arise, and when the mind ceases various dharmas cease

Translation: Therefore the three realms are an illusion (false and unreal), made only by the mind's imagining (entering the dream of ignorance, the six sense-object realms appear); apart from the mind there are no six sense-object realms (the dream of ignorance being awakened from, there are no six sense-object realms). What does this mean? Because all dharmas arise from the mind giving rise to false thoughts. All discrimination is merely the discrimination of one's own mind; mind does not see mind, and there is nothing to be apprehended. Know that all the realms of the world exist dependent upon the ignorant deluded mind (the dreaming mind) of sentient beings. Therefore all dharmas, like images in a mirror, have no substance to be apprehended; it is only the mind dreaming the dream of ignorance, because when the mind arises (entering the dream of ignorance) various dharmas arise (various realms appear), and when the mind ceases (the dream of ignorance awakened from) various dharmas cease (various realms cease).

[Therefore the three realms are false, made by mind alone; apart from mind there are no six sense-object realms] The three realms are doings within the dream of ignorance; once the dream is awakened from, there are no six sense-object realms.
Concerning
‘the three realms are false, made by mind alone’
and
‘when the mind arises various dharmas arise, when the mind ceases various dharmas cease’
, the Sutra of Divining Karmic Retribution (Zhan Cha Shan'e Yebao Jing) says:
‘Furthermore, know that the forms outside the mind
(the forms of the external realms within the mind)
like the various realms seen in a dream,
are made only by the mind's thought
(what the dreaming mind sees)
, with no real external events. All realms are likewise, for they all arise dependent upon seeing within
the dream of ignorance-consciousness
, being produced by false imagining
(this is what false imagining produces)
. Moreover, know that the inner mind is unceasing from thought to thought
(gross thought, subtle thought, or the subtlest thought, thought following thought without break)
, so that all realms seen and perceived likewise follow the mind in unceasing thought after thought
(continuing without break)
, according to the saying:
When the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease.’
[When the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease]

‘When the mind arises, various dharmas arise’ means that the mind arises (the initial stirring of thought) and one enters the dream of ignorance, so various dharmas appear; ‘when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease’ means that the mind ceases (the subtlest thought ceases) and the dream of ignorance is awakened from, so the various dharmas seen in the dream cease. Therefore ‘mind arises’ here refers to the initial stirring of thought, and ‘mind ceases’ refers to the cessation of the subtlest thought.
[Initial stirring of thought] This is

fundamental ignorance, also called beginningless ignorance. By this single stirring of thought one enters the dream of ignorance, dazed through the long night, unable to understand the truth, and so gives rise to delusion and creates karma, and thereby receives karmic retribution and turns about in birth and death. [Subtle thought] The subtle arising and ceasing of the consciousness-mind, which is the mark of the ālaya-vijñāna. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
‘When the bodhisattva's stage is exhausted
(having completed the ten stages)

, and the expedient means are fulfilled, then in a single thought of responding the awakening mind first arises, and the mind has no first mark; because one is far from subtle thought, one sees the mind-nature, and the mind is then forever abiding — this is called ultimate awakening.’
Q: Since all dharmas are illusory, body and mind are also illusions, and practice is also an illusion, then why practice? And who practices?

Answer: Although we are in the dream of ignorance and all dharmas are illusory, your actual experience is nonetheless very real: birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, worry, calamities from heaven, disasters from men — none of these feels in the least illusory to you, just as when you are in a night dream and have not yet awakened. Therefore the purpose of practice is to awaken from the dream of ignorance (to attain Buddhahood), thoroughly to escape these sufferings of life after life, and to save and deliver all sentient beings who undergo such suffering. Practice is the self-nature's own practicing — it is using illusion to train away illusion, so that when illusion is exhausted the dream awakens. This principle the Buddha sets forth incisively in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment; see, in
A Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment
, the chapter on the ‘illusion-like samādhi.’

Since one practices illusion with illusion, and the aim is that illusion be exhausted and the dream awaken, one must not practice apart from the phenomenal matters within the dream of ignorance, and yet one must not be deluded by the phenomenal matters and cling to them as real.

In practice there are frequently two deviations: first, leaning toward non-existence, denying the phenomenal matters and falling into annihilation; second, clinging to existence, deluded by phenomenal matters as real and being carried about by them. What is right is the Middle Way, which leans neither to non-existence nor to attachment: earnestly practice the six perfections and the myriad conducts while at the same time being free of appearances. Therefore in the sutras and treatises the teaching is often set forth simultaneously from the two viewpoints of the real mark of all dharmas and of the phenomenal matters of the dream of ignorance (the six sense-object realms). If one does not grasp this point, one is forever beset by doubt: why speak of non-existence at one moment and of existence at the next? Is it ultimately non-existence, or existence? In truth, ‘non-existence’ is spoken with regard to the essence and nature (the essential nature) — this is the real mark of all dharmas, what is called ‘serenely unborn, all dharmas one mark’; ‘existence’ is spoken with regard to the phenomenal matters of the dream of ignorance (the six sense-object realms), what is called ‘a many-splendored array of myriad phenomena, arising and ceasing in full array.’

[The Middle Way] Not leaning to non-existence, not leaning to existence; neither non-existence nor existence, yet also neither without non-existence nor without existence; not falling into either extreme; perfectly fused and unobstructed — this is called the Middle Way.

A thing has three aspects: essence, form, and function. The essence is the essential nature, also called the nature or the essence-nature; the essence of a thing is utterly empty, wholly without anything, and this is the common real mark of all dharmas, often described with words such as ‘true thusness is equal, unborn and unceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing, ultimately ever-present.’ ‘True thusness is equal’ means that the essence-nature (true thusness) of all dharmas is equal to one another, all alike being utterly empty and without anything; ‘unborn and unceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing, ultimately ever-present’ is a depiction of being utterly empty and without anything. The form is the appearance of the thing in the dream of ignorance, and the function is the working of the thing in the dream of ignorance.

[True thusness] Zhen (true) means real and genuine; ru (thusness) means abiding as always. The essence-nature of all dharmas, free of the false and real, is therefore called true; ever-abiding, unchanging and unaltered, it is therefore called thusness. [Unborn and unceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing, ultimately ever-present] ‘Unborn and unceasing’ — all dharmas are utterly empty, without anything; since they never existed at all, of course they are unborn and also unceasing. ‘Neither increasing nor decreasing’ — all dharmas are utterly empty, without anything, so of course there is no speaking of increase or decrease. ‘Ultimately ever-present’ — ‘ever-present’ describes there being no arising, ceasing, or change; all dharmas being utterly empty and without anything, they are naturally ultimately ever-present.

The Mahāyāna practitioner must both know the forms and functions and understand the essence-nature; must gather the forms back into the nature (gather the phenomenal matters back into the essence-nature), be free of appearances and without abiding, and not be turned by the realms.
As for the principle of being free of appearances and without abiding, the Buddha sets it forth very thoroughly in the Diamond Sutra, for example:
‘If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a lifespan, he is not a bodhisattva.’
This says that a bodhisattva must be free of the four marks.
‘If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are immeasurable.’

This says that giving should be free of marks. Because of the six perfections (giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajñā), giving ranks first, and here giving represents the six perfections.
‘A bodhisattva should be free of all marks and give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.’
This says: on the path of bodhi, from the very beginning, at the very moment of giving rise to the mind, one must be free of marks.
When Subhuti put the question:
‘World-Honored One! If a good man or good woman gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, on what should they abide? How should they subdue their mind?’
The Buddha answered:

‘A good man or good woman who gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should give rise to such a thought: I should bring all sentient beings to extinction, and having brought all sentient beings to extinction, there is yet not a single sentient being truly brought to extinction.’
So the answer to ‘On what should they abide? How should they subdue their mind?’ is: be free of appearances and without abiding, and so ferry sentient beings across.
‘One should not give rise to a mind abiding in forms, nor should one give rise to a mind abiding in sounds, scents, tastes, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.’
This says: do not give rise to mind by abiding in the sense-object realms, and when mind is given rise to, let it not abide in the sense-object realms.
‘By practicing all good dharmas with no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, one obtains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.’
This says: being free of the four marks and practicing any good dharma, one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

(This passage says that the key to attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is the absence of the four marks, and not the particular kind of good dharma one practices. The good dharma practiced without the four marks is the unconditioned dharma. The World-Honored One here reveals to us the universal principle of attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, from which we may also know how crucial and how important it is to be free of the four marks!)
